name: Roll from Chill Dog
summary: A safe reset from Chill Dog opens the high-leg control before any change of facing direction; the position does not itself require a rolling turtle escape.
description: A safe reset from Chill Dog opens the high-leg control before any change of facing direction; the position does not itself require a rolling turtle escape.
overview:
The bottom player is already facing the opponent in Chill Dog, with a high rubber-guard leg connection. No direct roll from the named high-guard configuration was established by the reviewed instruction. Do not roll onto the neck while retaining a loaded shoulder connection.

The bottom player is on the back or hip with a high rubber-guard leg across the upper back. One of the top player's arms is isolated beside the bottom player rather than framing inside. Release any wrist, neck or elbow loading before opening the high-leg enclosure. Lower the controlling leg through a comfortable hip angle rather than pulling the foot against the knee.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Brandon McCaghren — Gogoplata from rubber guard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wn39-wrfsbs); [Eddie Bravo — Chill Dog / Invisible Collar clarification](https://www.10thplanetjj.com/forum/threads/17657-Chill-Dog-Invisible-Collar-Question).

defender.description: Roll from Chill Dog (defender): Keep the free hand available for framing while preventing the isolated elbow from being pulled further away from your torso. The opponent changing the hand around your head signals the move beyond New York, not a turtle escape.
defender.overview:
The bottom player is already facing the opponent in Chill Dog, with a high rubber-guard leg connection. No direct roll from the named high-guard configuration was established by the reviewed instruction. Do not roll onto the neck while retaining a loaded shoulder connection.

Keep the free hand available for framing while preventing the isolated elbow from being pulled further away from your torso. The opponent changing the hand around your head signals the move beyond New York, not a turtle escape. Keep a safe base and prevent the free leg from closing high behind your head.

Recover the elbow toward your ribs only when the leg enclosure has slack, rather than jerking the shoulder. Bring the head and chest upright in stages after clearing the upper-body control. Do not drive the partner onto the neck or force the bent leg sideways to escape the control.
